Foreman records the rejection and continues awaiting drafter-f001-t002-d001's own terminal return. Nothing about the replacement's state changes, and no report content is read into the run.
assertions: The predecessor's lifecycle signal is recorded as an observation, not a backend return
It is explicitly not treated as idle_without_report
The late predecessor report is rejected on attribution despite being complete
The rejection is recorded and the active assignment's await continues unchanged
No content from the rejected report enters the run

evals.name: herdr-controller-lease-is-atomic-and-owner-bound
evals.prompt: $valcraft:foreman — on the herdr backend, two controllers start for the same project pool within the same second, and both observe the same session and pass every other readiness condition. State what decides which one proceeds and why an observational readiness check is not enough. Then resolve two later states: a lock whose recorded owner pane is still live in the named session, and a lock whose recorded owner pane no longer exists. Do not spawn workers or mutate files.
evals.expected_output: The atomic claim decides it: each controller attempts mkdir of .foreman/controller.lock, exactly one succeeds, and the loser fails readiness naming the recorded owner. An observational check cannot decide it because both controllers can observe an unheld pool simultaneously and both pass, so two runs would dispatch into the same pool and the same shared checkout. The winner writes its session, workspace, and pane id into the lock and releases it only as the recorded owner at run end. A lock whose owner pane is still live is held: never remove it, and fail readiness. A lock whose owner pane is absent from the named session is stale: record the observation and the reclaim in state.md, then take it — a reclaim without that record leaves no way to explain which controller owned the pool.
assertions: The atomic mkdir claim, not the readiness observation, decides which controller proceeds
The reason an observational check is insufficient is stated as simultaneous passing
The lock records owner session, workspace, and pane id and is released only by that owner
A live owner pane means the lock is held and readiness fails without removing it
A stale lock is reclaimed only after the observation and reclaim are recorded in state.md

evals.name: herdr-dispatch-records-skill-revision-or-says-unavailable
evals.prompt: $valcraft:foreman — on the herdr backend, record the dispatch checkpoint for a Draft assignment and a Forge assignment in the same run. The plugin's skills/index.json gives draft version 4f2b9c7d1a03e5b6 and the manifest release version reads 0.5.1. For the Forge dispatch, skills/index.json cannot be read. State exactly what each checkpoint records for the dispatched skill's revision. Do not spawn workers or mutate files.
evals.expected_output: The Draft checkpoint records 4f2b9c7d1a03e5b6 as the canonical revision, with 0.5.1 alongside it as corroborating metadata only. The release version never substitutes for the content hash, because two different snapshots can ship under one release version, so the hash is what distinguishes them. The Forge checkpoint records the revision as explicitly unavailable rather than falling back to the release version, the pane's skill base directory, or the Draft dispatch's hash: an unreadable index is a known gap, and a substituted value would make a later audit believe a revision was verified when it was not. The unavailability is stated in the checkpoint rather than left absent.
assertions: The Draft checkpoint records the content hash as the canonical revision
The release version is recorded only as corroborating metadata, never as the revision
The Forge checkpoint records the revision as explicitly unavailable
No fallback to the release version, base directory, or another dispatch's hash occurs
The unavailable state is written into the checkpoint rather than omitted

evals.name: herdr-retrospective-remediation-separates-the-two-reports
evals.prompt: $valcraft:foreman — on the herdr backend, RetroReview returns material findings R-001 and R-002 against Temper's retrospective PR. Dispatch the remediation. State which harness the remediating worker runs on, what physical identity and `.foreman` report path it receives, and which retrospective artifact it edits and where. Do not spawn workers or mutate files.
evals.expected_output: The remediating worker keeps the logical Temper identity and runs on Claude, the harness mapped to Temper, while RetroReview's closure check runs on Codex — the two never collapse onto one harness. It is a fresh physical worker: a new pane, a new agent name derived from the logical identity and the next dispatch ordinal, and a fresh, absent `.foreman` report path, because every dispatch gets a new physical identity and a predecessor must not be able to append to its replacement's active path. The retrospective artifact is the opposite case: Temper edits its existing report file under docs/retro/ in place, on its own unmerged branch, because a report becomes immutable only when its run ends. Foreman itself neither edits the report nor applies any proposal, and the two must not be confused — one is Foreman's coordination surface, the other is Temper's product.
assertions: The remediating worker keeps the Temper logical identity and runs on Claude
RetroReview's closure check stays on Codex rather than collapsing onto one harness
A fresh pane, agent name, and absent .foreman report path are assigned
The docs/retro report file is edited in place on the unmerged branch, not recreated
Foreman neither edits the retrospective report nor applies a proposal
